tagline: Reefs, rainforest and ancient Maya cities
overview:
On the Caribbean coast of Central America, wedged between Mexico and Guatemala, Belize is a small country where English is the official language, a legacy of its years as the colony of British Honduras. It covers about 23,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, and has only about 400,000 people, making it one of the least crowded countries in the Americas.

The capital is Belmopan, a small planned city built inland after Hurricane Hattie flattened much of coastal Belize City in 1961. Belize City remains the largest town and main port. Along the coast runs the Belize Barrier Reef, the second-longest coral reef in the world, dotted with hundreds of sandy islands called cayes.

Belizeans come from many roots: Maya, Kriol, Mestizo, Garifuna, Mennonite, East Indian and Chinese, and many people switch easily between English, Kriol and Spanish. Belize is an independent member of the Commonwealth with an elected parliament; the British monarch is head of state. Guatemala has long claimed part of its territory, a dispute the two countries have asked international judges to settle.
landAndNature:
The north of Belize is flat and swampy, threaded with lagoons and rivers, while the south rises into the Maya Mountains, where Doyle's Delight reaches about 1,124 meters. More than half the country is still covered by forest. The climate is hot and humid, with a rainy season from June to November and a risk of hurricanes.

Offshore, the reef shelters sea turtles, manatees, nurse sharks and rays, and the Great Blue Hole, a perfectly round sinkhole more than 120 meters deep, is a magnet for divers. Inland, the Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary was the world's first reserve created to protect jaguars. Black howler monkeys, which Belizeans call baboons, roar through the treetops, and the keel-billed toucan, the national bird, flashes its rainbow beak. Baird's tapir is the national animal.
peopleAndCulture:
Kriol, an English-based language with African and Spanish influences, is the everyday speech of most Belizeans, alongside English in schools and Spanish in many towns. The Garifuna people, descended from Africans and Caribbean islanders, keep their own language, drumming and punta dance; their arrival in 1832 is celebrated every November 19 on Garifuna Settlement Day.

Rice and beans cooked in coconut milk with stewed chicken is the national favorite, along with fry jacks (puffy fried dough) for breakfast and hudut, a Garifuna fish and plantain stew. Soccer, basketball and cycling are popular, and the Cross Country Cycling Classic each Easter crosses the whole country. The September Celebrations mix the anniversary of the 1798 Battle of St. George's Caye with Independence Day parades and carnival.
history:
Belize lay at the heart of the Maya world. Cities such as Caracol, Lamanai and Xunantunich flourished between about 250 and 900 AD, with pyramids taller than any modern building in the country. When Spanish explorers arrived in the 1500s the great cities were long abandoned, though Maya villages remained.

English loggers, known as Baymen, settled the coast in the 1600s to cut logwood and mahogany, bringing enslaved Africans to do the work. In 1798 they defeated a Spanish fleet at St. George's Caye. Britain declared the territory the colony of British Honduras in 1862. Slavery had ended in the 1830s, and later Garifuna, Mestizo and Mennonite communities arrived. The colony was renamed Belize in 1973 and became independent on September 21, 1981.
funFacts: The Great Blue Hole is so large and round that it can be seen clearly from space.
Belize is the only country in Central America where English is the official language.
The Maya city of Caracol was once bigger than modern Belize City and had a temple 43 meters high.
Belize's flag is one of the only national flags to show human figures, two woodcutters.
Baird's tapir, the national animal, can weigh 300 kilograms and is nicknamed the mountain cow.
The Cockscomb Basin, set aside in 1986, was the first jaguar reserve anywhere in the world.
